units.quote: (1) An applicant with a pending name change must not be issued a passport in her/his new name. See 8 FAM 1001.5 regarding applying for a replacement passport in a new name;
scope_quotes: c. The court order or decree must be final:
units.meaning: When an applicant has a pending name change rather than a final court order or decree, passport personnel must not issue a passport in the applicant's new name.

units.quote: (2) An applicant with a pending name change must not be issued a form FS-240 in her/his new name. See 8 FAM 1001.3 regarding amending a form FS-240; and
scope_quotes: c. The court order or decree must be final:
units.meaning: When an applicant has a pending name change rather than a final court order or decree, personnel must not issue a Form FS-240 in the applicant's new name.

units.quote: (3) You must clear the applicant's pending name even though the name change is not final and even if the passport is not being issued at this time.
scope_quotes: c. The court order or decree must be final:
units.meaning: Passport personnel must clear the applicant's pending name regardless of the fact that the name change is not final and even if a passport is not being issued at that time.

units.quote: d. The court order or decree must list both the applicant's current and former name(s).
units.meaning: A submitted court order or decree is required to list both the applicant's current name and their former name or names.

units.quote: EXCEPTION: You may receive a court order in which the applicant's former name is made confidential (e.g., California's Safe at Home program).
scope_quotes: d. The court order or decree must list both the applicant's current and former name(s).
units.meaning: As an exception to the requirement that a court order or decree list both the current and former name(s), personnel may receive a court order where the applicant's former name has been made confidential.

units.quote: When this occurs, the applicant must provide both her/his current and former names on the application.
scope_quotes: d. The court order or decree must list both the applicant's current and former name(s).
EXCEPTION: You may receive a court order in which the applicant's former name is made confidential (e.g., California's Safe at Home program).
units.meaning: When a court order renders the applicant's former name confidential, the applicant is obligated to provide both their current and former names on the passport application.

units.quote: You may request additional evidence of U.S. citizenship/non-citizen U.S. nationality or identity in accordance with 22 CFR 51.23 and 22 CFR 51.45.
scope_quotes: d. The court order or decree must list both the applicant's current and former name(s).
EXCEPTION: You may receive a court order in which the applicant's former name is made confidential (e.g., California's Safe at Home program).
units.meaning: When processing a court order with a confidential former name, personnel are authorized to request additional evidence of U.S. citizenship, non-citizen U.S. nationality, or identity under 22 CFR 51.23 and 22 CFR 51.45.

units.quote:
8 FAM 403.1-3(B) Name Spacing

(CT:CITZ-96; 08-04-2023)
units.meaning: Provides the section title and administrative transmittal metadata with no operational rights or duties.

units.quote: a. In accordance with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) recommendations, U.S. passports, form FS-240, and form DS-2060 are printed in all uppercase letters.
units.meaning: Pursuant to ICAO recommendations, all U.S. passports, Form FS-240, and Form DS-2060 are produced with text in all uppercase letters.

units.quote: Printing a name with multiple parts in uppercase letters causes the name to appear as one word unless the parts are separated with spaces.
units.meaning: Explains the formatting reality that uppercase printing of multi-part names merges parts into a single word unless spaces are inserted between the parts.

units.quote: Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:
units.meaning: Personnel are required to make a determination on how a multi-part name will appear on the issued document.

units.quote: (1) If the applicant's previous passport had a space, you should add a space on the current application;
scope_quotes: Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:
units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multi-part name, personnel should add a space on the current application if the applicant's previous passport contained a space.

units.quote: (2) If the applicant does not have a previous passport and the applicant's evidence of U.S. citizenship/non-citizen U.S. nationality or ID has a space, you should add a space on the current application; or
scope_quotes: Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:
units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multi-part name for an applicant lacking a previous passport, personnel should add a space on the current application if their citizenship/nationality evidence or ID has a space.

units.quote: (3) If the applicant expresses a clear preference to add or remove space, either verbally or in writing, you may add or remove it per the applicant's preference.
scope_quotes: Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:
units.meaning: When an applicant explicitly communicates a preference verbally or in writing to add or remove spacing in a multi-part name, personnel are permitted to add or remove spacing according to that preference.

units.quote: NOTE: If you receive applications from several family members, you should space the last names consistently, unless a family member expresses a clear preference for a different spacing.
units.meaning: Personnel should maintain consistent spacing across last names when receiving applications from multiple family members, unless an individual family member explicitly indicates a clear preference for alternative spacing.

units.quote: NOTE: For special-issuance passports, the spacing of an eligible family member's last name should match the spacing of the last name of the sponsor.
units.meaning: On special-issuance passports, the last name spacing for an eligible family member should conform to the spacing used in the sponsor's last name.

units.quote: b. Name spacing issues are generally not sufficient cause to rewrite a passport, unless the Department disregarded the applicant's clear preference (see 8 FAM 1001.2).
units.meaning: Issues regarding name spacing generally do not justify rewriting a passport, except when the Department failed to honor the applicant's clearly expressed preference.

units.quote: c. Arabic ordinal numbers must be changed to Roman numerals, for example, 2nd to II, 3rd to III:
units.meaning: Personnel are required to convert Arabic ordinal numbers in names into Roman numerals (such as converting 2nd to II, and 3rd to III).

units.quote: d. Some applicants may include the prefix “Sr.” as an abbreviation for “Señor” in Spanish meaning “Mr.” or “Mister” in English.
units.meaning: Notes that applicants may use the prefix 'Sr.' to represent the Spanish title 'Señor' rather than an English suffix.

units.quote: If you determine that this is the case, follow the guidance in 8 FAM 403.1-5(C) regarding ranks and titles.
scope_quotes: d. Some applicants may include the prefix “Sr.” as an abbreviation for “Señor” in Spanish meaning “Mr.” or “Mister” in English.
units.meaning: If personnel determine that 'Sr.' is used as an abbreviation for 'Señor', they must follow the instructions governing ranks and titles in 8 FAM 403.1-5(C).

units.quote: e. Name suffix issues are generally not sufficient cause to rewrite a passport, unless the Department disregarded the applicant's clear preference (see 8 FAM 1001.2).
units.meaning: Issues concerning name suffixes generally do not constitute sufficient reason to rewrite a passport, unless the Department failed to follow the applicant's clearly expressed preference.
